mainTopic: The penalty on a Jew whose slave ends up with a גוי: forced loss, partial sales, the size of the fine, and whether it passes to an heir
overview: This amud is about the חכמים's penalty on a Jew whose slave ends up in a גוי's hands. First the גמרא gives another explanation of the earlier case of a slave used as security for a loan. Then a ברייתא teaches that a slave collected by a גוי for a debt, or taken by a סיקריקון, does not go free. The גמרא defends this ruling against a ברייתא about grain seized by the king's officers and against רב's ruling about selling a slave to a gentile official. רבי ירמיה then asks about temporary sales, partial sales, and different kinds of buyers; only the גר תושב question is answered. רבי אמי rules that a master may take money for a slave who ran off to a foreign army, because he is only rescuing what he can. רבי יהושע בן לוי fines one who sells his slave to a גוי, and the גמרא brings two versions of how large the fine is compared to ריש לקיש's fine for selling an animal. The amud ends with רבי ירמיה asking whether the son is fined after his father dies. That question continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Another explanation: he agreed it could be taken, but it was not yet taken
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא offers a second answer to the earlier difficulty. The case is one where the Jew borrowed on the condition that the gentile could collect the slave or field, but the gentile had not collected it yet.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say instead: the case is where he borrowed on the condition that they would take it as payment, but they had not yet taken it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a different answer ("if you want, say") to the question it was just working on, about a slave or field used as security for a gentile's loan.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this case the gentile has not actually collected the field yet, so the field is still exempt from מעשר. But for the slave, the Jew's agreement to let him be collected is already enough for the חכמים to apply their penalty, so the slave goes free.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say: introduces an alternative answer
On condition that
To take it as collateral or collect it as payment

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the penalty on the slave can apply even before the gentile actually takes him. The Jew's agreement alone is enough.

phrases.english: And if you want, say:
where he borrowed on the condition that they would collect it,
phrases.notes: "It" means the slave or the field he put up as security for the loan.

phrases.english: but they did not yet collect it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer to the difficulty discussed just before this section.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One might think the slave and the field must be treated the same way.
steps.terutzMaskana: The case is one where collection was agreed to but has not happened. So the field stays exempt from מעשר, while the slave goes free as a penalty.

steps.title: A slave taken for a debt or by a robber does not go free
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that if a gentile collected a slave for a debt, or a סיקריקון took him by force, the slave does not go free.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים taught: if a gentile collected him for his debt, or a סיקריקון took him, he does not go out to freedom.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about cases where a slave ends up with a gentile without his master choosing to sell him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, a Jew who sells his slave to a gentile is penalized, and the slave goes free. Here the master did not sell the slave. The slave was collected for a debt or taken by force, so the חכמים did not penalize the master.

keyTerms.meaning: The חכמים taught: introduces a ברייתא
Collected him as payment of his debt
A violent person who forced people to give up their property
Goes out to freedom (the slave is freed)

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
If [a gentile] collected him for his debt,
or a violent robber took him,
he does not go out to freedom.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic with a ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A slave collected by a gentile for a debt, or seized by a סיקריקון, is not freed.

steps.title: Challenge: taking property for a debt seems to count like a sale
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions the 'debt' part of the ברייתא. Another ברייתא says that if the king's officers seized a threshing floor for a debt, the owner must tithe the grain. That suggests collecting for a debt is like a sale.
steps.simpleTranslation: And when collected for his debt, he does not go free?! Contrast it with this: if the king's household seized someone's threshing floor, then if it was for his debt, he must tithe; if it was unjust seizure, he is exempt from tithing!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how a slave taken for a debt can stay a slave. It points to a ברייתא about seized grain that seems to say the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the grain case, when the king takes the grain for a debt, the owner has to separate מעשר. This treats it as if he paid his debt with the grain, like a sale. If so, a slave taken for a debt should also count like a sale to a gentile, and the slave should go free.

keyTerms.meaning: And contrast it with: introduces a contradicting source
The king's household (royal officers)
Threshing floor
Unjust seizure, taking by force with no legal claim
To separate מעשר (tithe)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two kinds of seizure. Taken 'for his debt' means he owes tithes. Taken by אנפרות (plain robbery) means he is exempt.

phrases.english: And when taken for his debt, he does not [go free]?!
And contrast it with this:
one whose threshing floor the king's household seized by force,
if it was for his debt, he is obligated to tithe;
if it was unjust seizure, he is exempt from tithing!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the first half of the ברייתא in step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that a slave collected for a debt does not go free.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The grain ברייתא treats seizure for a debt like a sale, since the owner must tithe. So a slave collected for a debt should count as sold to a gentile and go free.

steps.title: The grain case is different because the owner gains from it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that in the grain case, the owner benefits from the seizure. That is why he must tithe. With the slave there is no such gain, so there is no penalty.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is different there, because he gains from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the contradiction by showing how the grain case differs from the slave case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With the grain, the owner pays part of his debt using grain that includes tithe, so he comes out ahead. That is why he must separate מעשר. With the slave, the master gains nothing from the seizure, so the חכמים did not penalize him, and the slave stays a slave.

keyTerms.meaning: It is different there
He profits from it, he comes out ahead

steps.whatToRemember: A slave collected for a debt does not go free. The grain case is different only because the owner gains from paying his debt with untithed grain.

phrases.english: It is different there,
phrases.notes: "There" means the threshing floor seized by the king's officers.

phrases.english: because he gains from it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 3.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Seizure for a debt always counts like a sale.
steps.terutzMaskana: The tithe obligation comes from the owner's gain, not from seizure being a sale. So the slave is not freed.

steps.title: רב's case of selling a slave to a gentile official
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges step 4 using רב's ruling that a slave sold to a gentile official goes free.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear, for רב said: One who sells his slave to a gentile official, the slave goes free!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings רב's ruling to attack the answer from step 4.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 4 said that an owner who gains nothing from the slave leaving his hands is not penalized. But an owner who sells to a pushy gentile official was pressured and probably did not want the sale. Even so, רב says the slave goes free, so the owner is penalized.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear: the גמרא is bringing a source
A government official
He goes free

phrases.english: Come and hear, for רב said:
One who sells his slave to a gentile official,
the slave goes free!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the 'no gain, no penalty' answer of step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that there is no penalty where the owner gains nothing
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The owner selling to an official is pressured and gains nothing, yet רב penalizes him.

steps.title: He should have calmed the official
steps.stepSummary: There the owner could have calmed the official some other way and did not.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, he should have calmed him down, and he did not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the official's case is different because the owner had another option.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner could have satisfied the official in another way, such as with a gift, so he would not take the slave. Since he failed to do that, he carries some blame and is penalized. The rule from step 4 still holds for cases like a debt collection, where the owner had no such option.

keyTerms.meaning: To calm down, to win someone over

phrases.english: There, he should have calmed him down,
phrases.notes: He means: calm the official in some other way so he would not take the slave.

phrases.english: and he did not calm him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 5.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Selling to an official is a forced sale with no gain, just like debt collection.
steps.terutzMaskana: The owner could have avoided the official's sale, so he is at fault. Debt collection had no such escape.

steps.title: רב's ruling quoted on its own
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to examine רב's ruling by itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: The matter itself: רב said: One who sells his slave to a gentile official, the slave goes free.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes רב's statement again so it can discuss it directly. It is setting up the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word גופא tells us the גמרא is turning to look closely at a statement it already mentioned in passing. Here רב's ruling becomes the main subject.

keyTerms.meaning: The matter itself: the גמרא returns to examine a quoted statement

phrases.english: The matter itself: רב said:
One who sells his slave to a gentile official,
the slave goes free.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns to examine the source cited in step 5.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A slave sold to a gentile official goes free.

steps.title: What could the owner have done?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the owner is penalized if he was forced.
steps.simpleTranslation: What could he have done?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how it is fair to penalize an owner who was forced by an official.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A penalty usually assumes the person did something wrong. If the official forced the sale, it seems the owner had no choice.

keyTerms.meaning: What could he have done?

phrases.english: What could he have done?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the fairness of רב's ruling in step 7.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why a pressured owner deserves a penalty

steps.title: He could have calmed the official
steps.stepSummary: The owner should have calmed the official some other way.
steps.simpleTranslation: He should have calmed him down, and he did not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the owner did have an option and did not use it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This repeats the answer from step 6. The owner is penalized because he could have found another way to satisfy the official.

phrases.english: He should have calmed him down, and he did not.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The owner failed to calm the official another way, so he is at fault.

steps.title: A sale for only thirty days
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה asks whether selling a slave to a gentile for thirty days frees him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה asked: If he sold him for thirty days, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה raises a new question: does a temporary sale count as a sale for this penalty?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Maybe only a permanent sale takes the slave away from the מצוות, so only that should cause the penalty. On the other hand, even a short sale puts him in a gentile's hands.

keyTerms.meaning: Asks, raises a question
What is the law?

phrases.english: רבי ירמיה asked:
If he sold him for thirty days, what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new question about how far the penalty reaches.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a temporary sale to a gentile frees the slave

steps.title: Trying to prove it from רב
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries to settle the question from רב's ruling about the official.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear, for רב said: One who sells his slave to a gentile official, the slave goes free!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings רב's ruling again, this time as a proof for רבי ירמיה's question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is that an official takes a slave only for a limited time or a specific job. If the slave still goes free there, then a thirty-day sale should also free him.

phrases.english: Come and hear, for רב said:
One who sells his slave to a gentile official,
the slave goes free!
phrases.notes: The proof assumes the official took the slave only for a while.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to answer step 10.
steps.raayaObject: A temporary sale frees the slave
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב's ruling about selling to a gentile official

steps.title: The official never gives the slave back
steps.stepSummary: The proof fails because a sale to an official is never reversed.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, it is a gentile official, whose sale is not reversed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof, so רבי ירמיה's question stays open.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In practice, an official does not return what he took, so that sale is really permanent. A true thirty-day sale, where the slave comes back, is a different case.

keyTerms.meaning: That does not get reversed, does not come back

phrases.english: There, it is a gentile official,
whose sale is not reversed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof in step 11.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof only; the thirty-day question stays unanswered
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The official's sale is actually permanent, so it cannot teach us about a temporary sale.

steps.title: Partial sales and different buyers
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה asks about sales that hold back part of the slave, and about different kinds of buyers.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he sold him except for his labor, what is the law? Except for the מצוות, what is the law? Except for שבתות and ימים טובים, what is the law? To a גר תושב, or to a ישראל משומד, what is the law? To a כותי, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא lists more questions to find the edges of the penalty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first three questions ask whether the penalty applies when the sale leaves the slave's work for his old master, or his מצוות, or his holy days. The last questions ask whether selling to a buyer who is partly connected to Torah life counts like selling to a regular גוי.

keyTerms.meaning: Except for his labor
A gentile who keeps the seven Noahide מצוות
A Jew who has abandoned Torah observance
A Samaritan

phrases.english: If he sold him except for his labor, what is the law?
phrases.notes: The gentile owns him, but the slave still works for his Jewish master.

phrases.english: Except for the מצוות, what is the law?
Except for שבתות and ימים טובים, what is the law?
To a גר תושב, or to a ישראל משומד, what is the law?
To a כותי, what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רבי ירמיה's questions about the limits of the penalty.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether partial sales, or sales to these kinds of buyers, free the slave

steps.title: At least the גר תושב question is answered
steps.stepSummary: A גר תושב counts as a גוי. About a כותי and a ישראל משומד, there are two opinions.
steps.simpleTranslation: Resolve at least one: a גר תושב is like a גוי. A כותי and a ישראל משומד: some say like a גוי, and some say like a Jew.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers one of the questions. Selling to a גר תושב frees the slave, just like selling to a גוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A גר תושב keeps only the Noahide laws, so a slave in his hands loses the מצוות just as with any גוי. For a כותי and a ישראל משומד the opinions are split, so the penalty depends on which view you follow. The questions about partial sales get no answer here.

keyTerms.meaning: Resolve at least one of the questions
Some say

steps.whatToRemember: Selling a slave to a גוי frees him as a penalty, except where the owner truly had no choice and gained nothing. The official's case counts because the owner could have calmed him. A גר תושב counts as a גוי, while the כותי and ישראל משומד are in dispute.
steps.confusionAlert: Only the גר תושב question is actually answered. The thirty-day question and the partial-sale questions are left open.

phrases.english: Resolve at least one:
a גר תושב is like a גוי.
A כותי and a ישראל משומד:
some say they are like a גוי,
and some say they are like a Jew.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers one of the questions from step 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A גר תושב is like a גוי. Whether a כותי or a ישראל משומד is like a גוי is disputed.

steps.title: May the master take payment for a slave who joined an army?
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי is asked whether a master may accept the value of a runaway slave who joined a foreign army and cannot be recovered.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked רבי אמי: a slave threw himself into the foreign armies, and his master cannot get him back, not through Jewish courts and not through gentile courts. May the master take the slave's value?
steps.whatsHappening: A new question is put to רבי אמי. A slave ran off to a foreign army and the master cannot get him back. May the master at least take money for him?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Selling a slave to a גוי is not allowed. So the worry is that taking money now would look like a sale. But here the master is not choosing to give the slave away; the slave is already lost to him.

keyTerms.meaning: They asked him (a question was raised before him)
Threw himself into the armies (ran off to join foreign troops)
The nations of the world (the non-Jewish nations)
His value; the money he is worth

phrases.english: They asked of Rabbi Ami:
A slave who threw himself into the armies,
and his master cannot get him out,
not through Jewish law
and not through the laws of the nations of the world,
what is the law: may he take his value?
phrases.notes: He means: may the master accept money from the army for the slave?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new question that grows out of the ban on selling a slave to a גוי, which has been under discussion in the earlier steps.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether taking payment for a slave lost to a foreign army counts as a forbidden sale to a גוי, or is allowed because the master has no other way to recover anything.

steps.title: A proof from a house that a gentile seized
steps.stepSummary: רבי זריקא finds a ברייתא that allows taking payment for a house a gentile seized by force, and this seems to answer the slave question.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה told רבי זריקא: go look through your collection of teachings. He went, searched, and found a ברייתא: if a person sells his house to a גוי, the money is forbidden. But if a גוי took a Jew's house by force, and the owner cannot get it back through Jewish or gentile courts, he may take its value. He may even write a document and register it in their courts, because he is like someone saving what he can from their hands.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זריקא finds a ברייתא about a house that a גוי seized by force. It says the owner may take money for it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא makes a clear split. A willing sale to a גוי is penalized, and the money is forbidden. A forced loss is different: taking money only saves what is left, so it is allowed. The slave in the army looks like the forced-loss case, so the master should be allowed to take money too.

keyTerms.meaning: Look in your collection of teachings (the ברייתות you know)
Took by force
Gentile courts
Like one who rescues something from their hands

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה לְרַבִּי זְרִיקָא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya said to Rabbi Zerika:
Go out and look in your collection of teachings.
He went out, searched carefully, and found that it is taught in a ברייתא:
One who sells his house to a gentile, its money is forbidden.
And a gentile who seized a Jew's house by force,
and its owner cannot get it back,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא בְּדִינֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְלֹא בְּדִינֵי אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם,
phrases.english: not through Jewish law and not through the laws of the nations of the world,
he is permitted to take its value,
and he may write a document and register it in their courts,
because he is like one who rescues from their hands.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to answer the question in step 15 by comparing it to a ברייתא about a seized house.
steps.raayaObject: That a master may take the value of a slave who is lost to a foreign army.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא: if a גוי seized a Jew's house and it cannot be recovered, the owner may take its value, because he is rescuing what he can.

steps.title: A house may be different from a slave
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back: a person needs a house and would never sell it willingly, but a person can live without a slave and might sell him, so the leniency may not carry over.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe that is only true of a house. Since a person cannot manage without a house, he will not come to sell it. But a slave, whom a person can manage without, he might come to sell. Or maybe there is no difference.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the proof. A house and a slave may not be comparable, so this proof does not settle the question. רבי אמי's ruling in the next step answers it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a house, nobody will use the leniency as a cover for a real sale, because people need their homes. Someone can live without a slave, though, so allowing payment might lead people to sell slaves to גוים. That would make it fitting to be strict. The words "או לא" mean the גמרא is not sure, so this proof alone cannot decide; step 18 gives the answer.

keyTerms.meaning: But perhaps
These words apply (only in this case)
He can manage; it is enough for him
To sell it (or him)

phrases.english: But perhaps this applies only to a house,

phrases.aramaic: דְּכֵיוָן דְּלָא סַגִּי לֵיהּ בְּלֹא בַּיִת,
phrases.english: since he cannot manage without a house,
he will not come to sell it;

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל עַבְדָּא – דְּסַגִּי לֵיהּ בְּלָא עַבְדָּא,
phrases.english: but a slave, whom he can manage without,
he might come to sell him. Or maybe not.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Weakens the proof from the house in step 16 by showing a possible difference between a house and a slave.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the comparison. The house ruling itself stands, and this proof does not settle the slave question (step 18 settles it).
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A house is a basic need, so no one would really sell it. A slave is not a basic need, so a lenient rule might lead people to sell slaves to גוים.

steps.title: רבי אמי's public ruling: the master may take the money
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי sends out a formal ruling to all of Israel: the master may take the slave's value and register it in gentile courts, because he is rescuing what he can.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אמי sent them a message: from me, אמי בר נתן, Torah goes out to all of Israel. A slave who threw himself into the foreign armies, whose master cannot get him back through Jewish or gentile law, the master may take his value. He may write a document and register it in the gentile courts, because he is like someone rescuing from their hands.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אמי gives the final answer to the question from step 15. The master is allowed to take the money for the slave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אמי rules the same way as the house ברייתא, even after the worry raised in step 17. Since the slave is already lost, taking money is treated as saving what is left, not as a sale. He announces it formally to all of Israel, so it is a clear ruling for everyone.

keyTerms.meaning: He sent to them (a written message)
Torah goes out to all of Israel (a formal public ruling)
Writes a document and registers it

steps.whatToRemember: If a slave runs off to a foreign army and cannot be recovered, his master may take his value, even through gentile courts. This is not a forbidden sale; he is only rescuing what he can from their hands.
steps.whyThisMatters: It sets the line between a willing sale to a גוי, which is penalized, and a forced loss, where taking payment is allowed.

phrases.english: Rabbi Ami sent to them:
"From me, Ami bar Natan,
Torah goes out to all of Israel:
phrases.notes: A formal way of saying this is a firm ruling for everyone.

phrases.english: A slave who threw himself into the armies,
and his master cannot get him out,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא בְּדִינֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְלֹא בְּדִינֵי אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם,
phrases.english: not through Jewish law and not through the laws of the nations of the world,
is permitted to take his value,
and he may write a document and register it in the courts of the gentiles,
because he is like one who rescues from their hands.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Settles the question that step 17 left open, ruling leniently just like the house case.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The master may take the slave's value and register it in gentile courts, because it counts as rescuing what he can, not as selling.

steps.title: Selling a slave to a gentile: fined up to one hundred times
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן לוי rules that someone who sells his slave to a גוי is fined up to one hundred times the slave's value.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע בן לוי said: Someone who sells his slave to a גוי is penalized up to one hundred times the slave's value.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new rule from רבי יהושע בן לוי: a master who sells his slave to a גוי gets a heavy fine, up to a hundred times the slave's price.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The topic moves from a slave the master lost against his will (the runaway who joined an army) to a slave the owner sold on purpose. Since the owner chose to do something wrong, חז״ל punish him heavily. He must buy the slave back from the גוי, even for up to a hundred times the price.

keyTerms.meaning: We fine or penalize. This is a punishment set by חז״ל.
Of his value, meaning the slave's price.
One who sells his slave to a non-Jew.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:
One who sells his slave to a gentile –
we penalize him
phrases.notes: The fine is that he has to buy the slave back from the גוי.

phrases.english: up to one hundred times his value.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי: הַמּוֹכֵר עַבְדּוֹ לְגוֹי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from a slave lost against the master's will (steps 15-18) to a slave sold on purpose to a גוי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who sells his slave to a גוי is fined up to one hundred times the slave's value.

steps.title: Is the number one hundred meant exactly?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether ריב״ל's 'one hundred' is a precise amount or just a way of saying 'a lot'.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is this exact, or not exact?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short question about the number in ריב״ל's rule. This sets up the proof that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sometimes a big number in the גמרא is just a way of saying 'a lot'. The גמרא wants to know whether 'one hundred' is a real legal limit or a loose expression.

keyTerms.meaning: Exactly, precisely as stated.
Not exact, a loose way of speaking.

phrases.english: Is it exact, or not exact?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions how precise the number in step 19 is.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is 'up to one hundred times' a precise legal figure or an exaggeration?

steps.title: Proof from ריש לקיש: selling a large animal is fined only up to ten
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests an answer from ריש לקיש, who fines someone who sells a large animal to a גוי only up to ten times its value.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: ריש לקיש said, someone who sells a large animal to a גוי is penalized up to ten times its value.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to answer the question by comparing to ריש לקיש's fine for selling a big animal to a גוי, which is only up to ten times its value.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If breaking the rule against selling an animal to a גוי is fined only up to ten times, then a slave might be fined the same way. That would mean ריב״ל's 'one hundred' is not exact.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear. This opens a proof from another source.
A large domestic animal, like a cow or a donkey.
The אמורא רבי שמעון בן לקיש.

phrases.english: Come and hear, for Reish Lakish said:
One who sells a large animal to a gentile –
we penalize him
up to ten times its value!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers an answer to the question of step 20.
steps.raayaObject: That ריב״ל's 'one hundred' is not exact, and the slave fine should match the animal fine.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ריש לקיש's rule: selling a large animal to a גוי is fined up to ten times its value.

steps.title: A slave is different because he loses מצוות every day
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof: a slave sold to a גוי is kept away from מצוות every single day, so his fine may be much bigger than an animal's.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe a slave is different, because every single day the owner takes him away from מצוות.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof. A slave cannot be compared to an animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A slave owned by a Jew keeps some מצוות. Once he is sold to a גוי, he loses them day after day. That ongoing spiritual loss can explain a bigger fine, so ריב״ל's 'one hundred' can still be exact.

keyTerms.meaning: It is different.
Removes or takes away.
Commandments.

phrases.english: But perhaps a slave is different,
since each and every day
he removes him from מצוות.
phrases.notes: 'He' is the owner who sold him, and 'him' is the slave.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of step 21.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The comparison between a slave and an animal.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A slave loses מצוות every day, which an animal does not, so a stricter fine for a slave makes sense.
steps.whatToRemember: In the first version: ריב״ל fines up to 100 for a slave, ריש לקיש fines up to 10 for an animal, and the two cannot be compared because a slave loses מצוות daily.

steps.title: Second version: ריב״ל says the fine is only up to ten
steps.stepSummary: Others report ריב״ל's rule differently: someone who sells his slave to a גוי is fined up to ten times his value.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: רבי יהושע בן לוי said, someone who sells his slave to a גוי is penalized up to ten times his value.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second version of the whole discussion. In this version ריב״ל's number is ten, not one hundred.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case is the same but the number is swapped. This changes what the question 'is it exact?' means. Now it asks whether ten is the most he can be fined, or whether he could be fined even more.

keyTerms.meaning: And some say. This introduces a different report of the same teaching.

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two versions. In version one, the slave is 100 and the animal is 10. In version two, it is the opposite: the slave is 10 and the animal is 100.

phrases.english: And there are those who say:
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:
One who sells his slave to a gentile –
we penalize him
up to ten times his value.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיכָּא דְאָמְרִי, אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Restates step 19 in a second version with a different number.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In this version, one who sells his slave to a גוי is fined up to ten times his value.

steps.title: Second version: is ten meant exactly?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks again whether the number, now ten, is exact.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is this exact, or not exact?
steps.whatsHappening: The same question is asked in the second version. This sets up the proof from ריש לקיש with the new numbers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the question means: is ten the limit, or could the fine go higher? The answer will come from comparing to an animal.

phrases.english: Is it exact, or not exact?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the precision of the number in step 23.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is 'up to ten times' the real upper limit of the slave fine?

steps.title: Second version: ריש לקיש fines up to one hundred for an animal
steps.stepSummary: In this version ריש לקיש fines someone who sells a large animal to a גוי up to one hundred times its value, which suggests ten is not the real limit for a slave.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: ריש לקיש said, someone who sells a large animal to a גוי is penalized up to one hundred times its value.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings ריש לקיש again, but now he fines up to a hundred times for an animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If selling an animal can cost up to a hundred times, then selling a slave, which is more serious, should cost at least that much. So ריב״ל's 'ten' seems not to be exact.

phrases.english: Come and hear, for Reish Lakish said:
One who sells a large animal to a gentile –
we penalize him
up to one hundred times its value!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers an answer to the question of step 24.
steps.raayaObject: That ריב״ל's 'ten' is not exact, and a slave's fine should be at least as large as an animal's.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ריש לקיש's rule in this version: selling a large animal to a גוי is fined up to one hundred times its value.

steps.title: A slave is different because he does not come back
steps.stepSummary: The proof from ריש לקיש's hundred-times fine for an animal is pushed off: a slave does not return to his owner, so his fine can be smaller.
steps.simpleTranslation: A slave is different, because he does not come back to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof from step 25. An animal and a slave are not the same, so their fines can be different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the master buys back an animal from the גוי, he keeps it again. When he buys back a slave, the slave goes free and does not come back to him. So חכמים may have fined him less for a slave, and the number ten can still be exact.

keyTerms.meaning: It is different
It comes back to him

phrases.english: A slave is different,
because he does not come back to him.
phrases.notes: Once the master buys him back from the גוי, the slave goes free. He does not go back to working for his old master.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof in step 25 by pointing out a difference between a slave and an animal.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The comparison between the animal fine and the slave fine
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: An animal returns to its owner after being bought back, but a slave goes free, so the fines do not have to match.

steps.title: That difference would only add one more
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the distinction: if the animal's fine is bigger only because it comes back, the fine should be just one extra measure, not ten times more.
steps.simpleTranslation: But for an animal, what is the reason for the bigger fine? Because it comes back to him? Then let him be fined only one more!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from step 26. It says this difference is far too small to explain the gap between ten and one hundred.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the animal's fine is bigger only because the owner gets the animal back, that gain is worth one animal. So the fine should be just one measure more, like eleven instead of ten. It does not explain jumping all the way to one hundred.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason?
Let him be fined
One more

phrases.english: But an animal, what is the reason?
Because it comes back to him?!
Then let him be fined just one more!
phrases.notes: He means one extra measure on top of the slave's fine, like eleven times instead of ten.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the distinction offered in step 26.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the slave's fine is smaller because he does not come back
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Getting the animal back is worth only one animal, so it could explain only one extra measure, not a hundred instead of ten.

steps.title: Selling a slave is uncommon, so חכמים did not decree a big fine
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives a new distinction: selling a slave to a גוי rarely happens, and חכמים do not make decrees for rare cases.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, selling a slave is something that does not happen often, and חכמים do not make decrees about something that does not happen often.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the first distinction and gives a new reason why the slave's fine can be smaller than the animal's.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Selling animals to a גוי happens often, so חכמים made a strong fine to stop it. Selling a slave is rare, and חכמים did not make the same strong decree for a rare case. So the animal case cannot prove anything about the slave's number.

keyTerms.meaning: Something that does not happen often
חכמים did not make a decree about it

steps.whatToRemember: A general rule: חכמים usually do not make decrees for uncommon situations. This is why the slave's fine is not as big as the animal's.
steps.whyThisMatters: The rule that חכמים do not decree in rare cases appears in many places in ש״ס, and here it explains why two similar fines are so different.

phrases.english: Rather, a slave is something uncommon,
phrases.notes: He means selling a slave to a גוי does not happen often.

phrases.english: and with something uncommon,
the Rabbis do not make a decree about it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the distinction rejected in step 27 with a new one.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The animal's hundred-times fine shows that ten is not the real limit for a slave.
steps.terutzMaskana: Selling a slave is rare, so חכמים did not decree a large fine for it. The animal case says nothing about the slave.

steps.title: Is the son fined after his father dies?
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה asks רבי אסי whether, if a man sold his slave to a גוי and died, his son must pay the fine. Even if a son is fined for his father's blemishing of a בכור, that is a Torah prohibition, while selling a slave is only rabbinic.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה asked רבי אסי: if a man sold his slave and died, do we fine his son after him? Even if you say that someone who cut the ear of a בכור and died, his son is fined after him, that is because it is a Torah prohibition. But here it is only a rabbinic prohibition.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question. רבי ירמיה asks whether the fine for selling a slave passes on to the seller's son after the seller dies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a known case where the son is fined. A father cut a בכור's ear to make it blemished, so it could be eaten, and then died. But that may be because blemishing a בכור is forbidden by the Torah. Selling a slave to a גוי is only forbidden by חכמים, so maybe the son is not fined.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked him
If you will say; even if you decide
Cut the ear of a firstborn animal
A prohibition from the Torah
A prohibition from חכמים

steps.confusionAlert: The בכור case is not the answer to the question. It only shows why the question is hard: even if the son is fined there, the slave case may be different.

phrases.aramaic: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה מֵרַבִּי אַסִּי:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya asked Rabbi Asi:
If he sold his slave and died,
what is the law, do they fine his son after him?
Even if you say:
"If he cut the ear of a firstborn animal and died,
phrases.notes: Cutting the ear gives the בכור a blemish, so it could be eaten. Doing this on purpose is forbidden.

phrases.english: they fine his son after him" —
that is because it is a Torah prohibition,
but here it is a rabbinic prohibition.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה מֵרַבִּי אַסִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new question about the slave-selling fine: does it pass to the heir?
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the son of a man who sold his slave to a גוי and died must still pay the fine and buy back the slave.
